at.step: Every range in this topic is written as a half-open interval [lo, hi): lo is always a candidate, hi is always one past the last candidate, and the loop invariant is kept at the top of every iteration — the answer, if it exists, lies in [lo, hi). A closed [lo, hi] version needs a fiddlier termination check, lo > hi instead of just lo == hi.

lower_bound is the first index with a[i] >= x; upper_bound is the first index with a[i] > x — the same loop with one comparison flipped. First and last occurrence of a key, and the count of a key, all reduce to one or both of them: on three equal 3s, lower_bound lands on the first, upper_bound one past the last, and their difference is the count.

syllabus.clause: the overflow-safe midpoint (the bug found in many libraries in 2006)

at.step: The naive midpoint, (low + high) / 2, shipped in Bentley's Programming Pearls and in the JDK's own Arrays.binarySearch — written by the engineer, Joshua Bloch, who later found the bug in his own code. Once low + high exceeds the maximum value a fixed-width signed integer can hold, the sum wraps negative, and the bug sat unnoticed for about nine years before it broke someone's program and was reported.

The identical overflow, reproduced on an eight-bit signed integer so the wraparound lands on indices small enough to read by hand: 70 + 90 = 160 exceeds the eight-bit signed maximum of 127, wraps to −96, and the naive midpoint comes out negative, −48, an out-of-bounds index. The safe line, low + ((high − low) / 2), never sums two large values and gives the correct 80.

Every iteration either returns or strictly shrinks hi − lo, since lo <= mid < hi whenever lo < hi: the range width can only fall, never stay put or rise, and it starts at n. That proves termination by itself — at most ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ iterations, twenty for a million keys, checked directly against every possible target, not assumed.
